# SSG-48 gripper

> Documentation for the SSG-48 adaptive electric gripper by Source Robotics.

Every page of this site is also available as Markdown at its address followed by `index.md`, with its links absolute; `llms-full.txt` holds every page in one file. The version box on the landing page names the release the pages describe.

Full text of every page, in the order of the site's navigation. Source: https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/

# SSG-48 Gripper Manual

![SSG-48 gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/hero.webp)

<div class="doc-meta" markdown>

**Document number:** SR-5004

**SSG-48 gripper release:** 2

**Firmware:** Spectral 110

**Revision:** 2026.E

**Published:** 2026-11-13

**Applies to:** SSG-48 gripper release 2 with the Spectral Micro driver PCB v2.0, Spectral firmware 110

*Original instructions*

</div>

[Quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/quick-start/) [About this manual](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/about/)

Source Robotics d.o.o. publishes this document for the SSG-48 adaptive electric gripper. It is revised as the gripper and its
firmware change; the document number, the gripper release, the firmware, the revision and the date above identify
the version you are reading, and the document history on the About page says what changed. The version selector
in the header switches between gripper releases. The gripper runs the Spectral Micro driver's firmware: take care that
the firmware named under *Applies to* matches what the gripper reports. The text and the images are licensed
CC BY-SA 4.0, the code examples MIT.

**The SSG-48 is open source, and that is important to us.** Everything the gripper is made of is published: the
CAD and print files, the bill of materials, the assembly instructions, the driver's firmware and the software that
drives it. Buy the gripper assembled, or build one yourself; change the jaws or the body for your application and
fit it to any robot. The [build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/build/) is the order to do it in.

# Quick start

From an assembled SSG-48 gripper to its first gentle open and close, using Motor GUI on a PC.
For a gripper already connected to a robot, use [On PAROL6 and PAR6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/robots/).

!!! danger "Before connecting power"
    Keep fingers and loose objects out of the stroke. Calibration opens and closes the jaws fully. A wrong
    cable can reverse the supply or put 24 V on a CAN pin, and either destroys the driver: check the [numbered pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/connector/#pin-numbers).

## 1. Choose your starting point

| Your gripper | Start here |
|---|---|
| Bought assembled | Its motor is already calibrated and the driver configured. Continue below; the jaws still need calibration after each power-up. |
| Self-built, or a replacement driver or motor | Finish [Driver setup and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/build/first-run/) first, then return here. Do not apply a factory preset to a bought gripper just to try this page. |
| No hardware yet | Open [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/), choose **Mock CAN (demo)** and **Connect**, then switch to **Gripper**. The demo is an SSG-48; the control panel is shared with MSG. |

## 2. Gather and mount

You need a mounted gripper with jaws/fingers fitted, a **24 V supply**, a correctly wired **M8 cable**, a
**CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter**, and Chrome or Edge.

1. Mount the gripper: [Mounting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/mounting/).
2. Fit the jaws: [Jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/jaws/).

!!! success "Check"
    The body cannot shift, the jaws travel freely, and the cable cannot enter their path.

More: the [What you need](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/01-overview/what-you-need/) page lists the parts.

## 3. Wire with power off

1. Check the cable against [Connector and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/connector/): gripper pin 1 is CANL,
   pin 2 CANH, pin 3 +24 V, pin 4 GND.

    ![M8 male on the gripper, as it sits in the gripper: the numbered signals](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/gripper-m8-face.svg){ width="520" }
    ![M8 male on the gripper, as it sits in the gripper: the numbered signals](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/gripper-m8-face_dark.svg){ width="520" }

2. Check continuity before the first power-up.
3. Connect the supply and the CANvas adapter as shown below.

    ```mermaid
    flowchart LR
        PC[PC USB] --> A[CANvas adapter]
        A -- CANH --> P2[Gripper pin 2: CANH]
        A -- CANL --> P1[Gripper pin 1: CANL]
        S[24 V supply] -- positive --> P3[Gripper pin 3: +24 V]
        S -- return --> P4[Gripper pin 4: GND]
    ```

4. Set the gripper's CAN termination ON for this two-node bench bus; the CANvas adapter provides the other end.
5. Leave the gripper at its shipped node ID, **0**, unless you already assigned another.

!!! success "Check, unpowered"
    The supply polarity and cable pinout match, and CANH-to-CANL measures about **60 Ω** with the bus connected.
    Otherwise check [The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/cable/) and [CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/can-termination/)
    before powering it.

## 4. Connect Motor GUI

1. Power the gripper.
2. Plug the CANvas adapter into USB.
3. Open [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/).
4. Choose **CAN (slcan)** at **1 Mbit/s**.
5. Press **Connect**, and choose the adapter's serial port.
6. Select node **0** (or your assigned ID).
7. Switch from **Motor** to **Gripper**.

!!! success "Check"
    Position and current feedback arrive. *Not calibrated* after power-up is normal. If feedback is missing, check
    the power, port, node ID and termination: [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/09-troubleshooting/). If a fault disables
    the controls, resolve it using [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/errors/).

More: the [illustrated Motor GUI guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/05-setup/motor-gui/) shows the panel.

## 5. Calibrate and activate

1. If the panel shows an error, press **Clear errors** first.
2. With the stroke empty and the gripper deactivated, press **Calibrate**.
3. Read the prompt, and press **Start calibration**.

    ![Mock gripper calibration prompt warning that the jaws travel through their full range](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/motor-gui/gripper-calibration-demo.jpg){ width="700" }

4. Let the jaws find both end stops, and press nothing else until the panel says **Calibrated**: a move or a clear
   during the calibration ends it.
5. Press **Activate**, and check for faults.

!!! success "Check"
    The panel says **Calibrated**, **Activated**, and **No errors** before you command a move. A calibration that
    times out after 30 seconds has not found its end stops; do not continue as if it passed. Use
    [Calibration troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/09-troubleshooting/#calibration).

More: [Calibrate, activate, move](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/05-setup/first-moves/), the full procedure.

## 6. Make the first move

1. Set **Speed 30**, and apply it with its **Set** button.
2. Set **Current 300 mA**, and apply it with its **Set** button.
3. Press **Open**, then **Close**.
4. After that works, put a light test object between the jaws and repeat, keeping fingers clear.

![Calibrated and activated gripper demo with command controls and plots](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/motor-gui/gripper-ready-demo.jpg){ width="700" }

!!! success "Check"
    The position follows the command, and **Open** and **Close** end *at position* without pressing on the
    stops; on an object the jaws stop before fully closed and the panel reports an object. If it does not move,
    slips or reports an error, use [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/09-troubleshooting/).

The current limit sets an approximate force limit; [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/)
explains the relationship and the motor's limits.

## 7. Finish and continue

Remove the test object before deactivating or switching off: the grip may release. Disconnect Motor GUI and
switch off the supply before changing cables.

| Next task | Guide |
|---|---|
| Control it from a program | [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/python/), [With ROS 2](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/ros2/) |
| Put it on a robot | [On PAROL6 and PAR6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/robots/) |
| Inspect a CAN frame or download DBC definitions | [CAN frame tool and downloads](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/reference/can-tools/) |
| Diagnose a problem | [Troubleshooting](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/09-troubleshooting/), [Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/errors/) |

# About this manual

The SSG-48 Gripper Manual covers the SSG-48 adaptive electric gripper from unpacking to a gripper that works on a robot: mounting and cabling, the
first setup with Motor GUI, control over CAN and UART, from Python, from ROS 2 and from the PAROL6 and PAR6
robots, and firmware updates. It is written for a maker, a student or an engineer who can plug in a cable and run
a Python script. Read [Safety](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/02-safety/) before you power anything; [First setup](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/05-setup/) is the
shortest path to a gripper that moves.

The gripper is a Spectral Micro BLDC driver in gripper mode. The driver itself, from its full command set to its calibration
and its bootloader, is documented on the [Spectral site](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/); this manual links there instead of
repeating it.

## Finding your way

Four tabs: **SSG-48 Gripper Manual**, the numbered chapters, read from the start; **API reference**, the gripper's CAN
messages, UART commands, status bits and Python calls, for looking things up (the driver's complete reference is on
the Spectral site); **Guides**, worked examples; **Support**, help and problem reports.

The dropdown next to the site name switches between gripper releases, and a page of an older release says so in a
bar at the top. The repository card in the header opens the product repository; every page ends with a link to
edit it and one to report a problem with it.
## Warnings and notes

!!! note "Note"
    Points out something that is easy to miss or that changes what follows: a default, a limit, a side effect.

!!! warning "Notice"
    The robot, the tool, or data on the control box can be damaged or lost if this is ignored. Nobody is at risk.

!!! danger "Danger"
    Someone can be injured if this is ignored. Stop and read the whole box before acting on the step it belongs to.

A document marked with a firmware release describes SSG-48 gripper release 2 running Spectral firmware 110. The version selector in the header switches between gripper releases; a new firmware release for the same gripper updates the pages in place. The compatibility table says which firmware, Python library and hardware revisions work together.

The driver inside the gripper is documented at [https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/). The MSG gripper, the SSG-48's successor on the STEPFOC stepper driver, is at [docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/). The robots the gripper is
made for: [docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/) and
[docs.source-robotics.com/par6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/par6/).

## Document history

The manual is versioned by gripper release, the version the product repository tags (the selector in the header);
within a release it follows the Spectral firmware the gripper runs, with a new revision letter per update. The
text and the images are licensed [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/), the code
examples [MIT](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG48-gripper-docs/blob/main/LICENSE-CODE); the hardware design is published under the CERN Open Hardware Licence v2, strongly reciprocal (CERN-OHL-S-2.0), in the
[product repository](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper). The Source Robotics name, the product names and the logos are not covered
by any of these.

| Revision | Date | Changes |
|---|---|---|
| 2026.E | 2026-11-13 | Spectral firmware 110: a move ends cleanly, with a few mA left (KI-11); a soft start; 0 and 255 reached without pressing on the stops, each end read under a light push (KI-12); an object reported after 50 ms of standstill; the gripper pushes with its own current and leaves the driver's limit alone (KI-13); the calibration restarts from the beginning and needs 1000 ticks of stroke (KI-3); brake or coast saved (KI-14); a watchdog that runs out while idle starts no hold (KI-15); parameters 90 to 93; `#Estop` over UART |
| 2026.D | 2026-11-10 | Spectral firmware 109: the generated CAN and UART reference; the SSG-48 preset's current gains on 109; a poll right after a move no longer cancels it (KI-10); calibration puts the current limit back (KI-5); the gripper's current clamped at 2800 mA. Python library 1.21, which reads the object detection right (KI-7) |
| 2026.C | 2026-11-05 | The M8 pinout corrected to the one the gripper is built with (1 +24 V, 2 CANL, 3 GND, 4 CANH; page 17 of the SSG-48 assembly manual): the pin table, its drawing and the quick start of 2026.B had all four pins wrong; the bootloader comes with Spectral release 104, the first built for it; the cable warnings: the other robot's cable reverses the supply, it does not put 24 V on the CAN pins; the PAROL6 cable's pin pairs |
| 2026.B | 2026-11-04 | Gripper release 2, with the files as downloads on the release; known issues; data for robot integration (frame, mass, inertia, TCP); check boxes after each step and Windows, Linux and macOS tabs; numbered figure captions; the downloads with their versions; safety at the jaws, static and cleaning; the thermistor and the thermal cement in the BOM; the hardware licence CERN-OHL-S-2.0 |
| 2026.A | 2026-11-03 | First version in this form: the manual chapters, the generated CAN and UART reference; gripper release 1.1, firmware 107 |

# Overview

What the SSG-48 gripper is and how it works, the versions of its hardware, and what you need around it to get it
gripping.

  ![The gripper in action](https://img.youtube.com/vi/DQgi8Ua-VAU/hqdefault.jpg){ width="480" }
  <figcaption><a href="https://www.youtube.com/shorts/DQgi8Ua-VAU">The video of the gripper in action</a>.</figcaption>
</figure>

- [Hardware versions](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/01-overview/hardware-versions/)

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/01-overview/gripper-at-a-glance/ -->

# The gripper at a glance

The SSG-48 is a two-jaw parallel gripper driven by a brushless gimbal motor under field-oriented control.

The
[Spectral Micro driver](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/) inside the body regulates the
motor's current, so a move sets not only where the jaws go and how fast, but how hard they press: the current
limit is the grip force, from about 8 N at 150 mA to about 80 N at 1500 mA.

The jaws stop on an object, hold it with that force, and the
driver reports that an object was found.

![The SSG-48 gripper with pinch fingers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/SSG48_gripper_angle.webp){ width="600" }

## The parts

| Part | What it does |
|---|---|
| GBM5208-75 gimbal motor | the actuator: a brushless motor wound for high torque at low speed and low current |
| Spectral Micro driver, inside the body | field-oriented control of the motor, the gripper state machine, the CAN and UART interfaces |
| Pinion on the motor, two racks on a linear rail | the pinion turns, the two racks move in opposite directions: the jaws open and close symmetrically |
| MGN7 linear rail, 100 mm | carries the two jaw plates; 48 mm of stroke |
| Jaw plates | printed, with a four-hole pattern for your own fingers; fin-ray and pinch fingers in the repository |
| Thermistor in the motor windings | temperature protection: the gripper stops at 75 °C |
| M8 4-pin connector | 24 V and the CAN bus, one cable to the robot |
| Coupler connector | mounts the gripper on the PAROL6 or PAR6 wrist, on a UR5 flange, or on your own with the template |

The driver's status LED, its UART port and its CAN termination switch are inside the body, under the coupler
connector.

## What the firmware does

After power-up the gripper calibrates by finding both end stops. Then it takes move commands: a position from 0
(open) to 255 (closed), a speed from 0 to 255 and a current limit in mA.

When the jaws stop short of the target
with the current at its limit, an object is in the way and is held; when they reach the target, the position is
held. Every answer carries the state: moving, object found while closing or opening, or at the position.

The
gripper stops itself on an over-temperature, an E-stop bit from the host, a CAN watchdog that runs out, and every
fault the driver detects. [How the gripper works](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/how-it-works/) and
[Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/errors/) have the details.

## How it is controlled

- **CAN**, 1 Mbit/s, on the same cable as the power: one message moves the gripper and is answered with its
  state. From a PC with the CANvas adapter, from a ROS 2 node, from PAROL6 or PAR6, or from your own controller.
  See [Over CAN](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/can/).
- **Python**, the `Spectral-BLDC` library on top of CAN. See [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/python/).
- **Motor GUI** in the browser: connect, calibrate, open and close, watch the plots. See [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/05-setup/motor-gui/).
- **UART**, the driver's serial port inside the body: for configuration, and for a self-built gripper. See
  [Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/uart/).

The [MSG gripper](https://docs.source-robotics.com/MSG-gripper-docs/) is the SSG-48's successor: the same
protocol and software, with a stepper and the STEPFOC driver, three rail lengths and a camera mount. Programs
written for one run on the other.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/01-overview/hardware-versions/ -->

# Hardware versions

The SSG-48 exists in two mechanical versions, both in the product repository's
[Print files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/tree/main/Print%20files):

| Version | Folder | What differs |
|---|---|---|
| V1 | `V1` | the original body, lid, gear and magnet shaft |
| V2 | `V2` | the "large bearing" body, lid, gear and magnet shaft: a larger bearing on the pinion for a stiffer, longer-lasting mechanism |

The electronics, the motor, the rail, the jaw plates, the coupler connectors and everything about control are the
same in both; a gripper from the shop is a V2. The product release V2 (November 2026) carries the parts of both
versions; the release V1.1 (2024) is the version tested with PAROL6.

The jaw plates, the coupler connectors (`coupler_connector_PAROL6`, `coupler_connector_PAR6`,
`connector_coupler_generic`) and the fingers are common to both versions.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/01-overview/what-you-need/ -->

# What you need

## The gripper

The SSG-48 is sold assembled, calibrated and configured in the [Source Robotics shop](https://source-robotics.com/products/compliant-gripper).
It ships with the current Spectral firmware and the bootloader installed, its driver in gripper mode and its motor
calibrated; the gripper calibration (finding the end stops) runs after every power-up and is part of normal use.

**Or build it.** The SSG-48 is open source, and that is important to us: the CAD and printable files, the bill of
materials, the assembly manual and video, the firmware and the software are all published.
[The build guide](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/build/) is the order to do it in.

## What is in the box

The gripper, assembled, calibrated and configured, in black or grey. **Not in the box:** the fingers, which you
print from the repository; the cable, sold separately; the 8 mm shaft coupler for a PAROL6, which you ask for
when ordering; a CAN adapter for a PC.

## A cable and a 24 V supply

The gripper is powered and controlled through one M8 4-pin cable: 24 V, GND, CANH, CANL.

| Where the gripper goes | Cable |
|---|---|
| PAROL6 | the [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) from the shop |
| PAR6 | the PAR6 gripper cable (the shop; coming soon), wired differently from the PAROL6 one |
| a bench, or your own robot | a cable you make from an M8 4-pin connector and four wires, see [The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/cable/) |

![PAROL6 and PAR6 gripper cables are not interchangeable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/cable_warning.svg){ width="1000" }

!!! danger "The two robot cables differ"
    PAROL6 and PAR6 put the four signals on different pins. A cable for the wrong robot, or a self-made cable with
    a wrong pin, puts 24 V where the CAN bus belongs and destroys the gripper's driver. Check the pinout before
    you plug in a cable for the first time.

On the bench, a 24 V supply with a current limit (2 A is plenty for one gripper) is the safest source.

## A CAN interface

The gripper talks CAN. On a robot, the robot's control board provides the bus. On a PC, the
[CANvas USB-to-CAN adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter) does; it shows up as a
serial port and works with Motor GUI, the Python library and the ROS 2 drivers. Any adapter that `python-can` supports works
with the library.

## Software

- **Motor GUI**, [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/), in the browser over the CANvas adapter: the recommended
  tool to test and set up a gripper, with a gripper panel for the SSG-48 and the MSG; see
  [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/05-setup/motor-gui/). The earlier [SSG-gripper-GUI](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-gripper-GUI),
  a Python program, is legacy.
- **Python**: `pip install Spectral-BLDC`, the library the ROS 2 drivers are built on; see
  [With Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/python/).
- **ROS 2**: the [ssg48_adaptive_electric_gripper_ros2](https://github.com/Lass6230/ssg48_adaptive_electric_gripper_ros2)
  package, or the MSG gripper's driver, which speaks the same protocol; see [With ROS 2](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/ros2/).
- **PAROL6 and PAR6**: the robots' own software drives the gripper; see [On PAROL6 and PAR6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/robots/).
- **For a self-built gripper**: a 3.3 V USB-to-serial adapter ([serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter))
  for the driver's UART port, to configure the driver with Motor GUI or a terminal; see
  [Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/build/first-run/). For a self-build we recommend the
  [Spectral Micro BLDC starter kit](https://source-robotics.com/products/spectral-micro-bldc-starter-kit): it has this adapter and the rest of what the driver's setup needs
  ([Kits and the shop](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/build/#kits-and-the-shop)).

## Optional

- **Fingers** for your objects: the fin-ray and pinch fingers in the repository, or your own on the jaw plate
  template; see [Jaws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/jaws/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/02-safety/ -->

# Safety

The SSG-48 gripper is a force-controlled gripper for collaborative and research robots, not a certified safety
component. Whoever puts it on a machine is responsible for the risk assessment of the gripper, the robot and
everything around them. Read this chapter before you power the gripper; the rules here are the ones that injure a
hand or destroy the gripper when they are ignored.

## Mechanical

!!! danger "The jaws"
    The jaws are a pinch point. At a high current limit they close with up to 80 N, enough to crush a finger, and
    at full speed they travel the whole stroke in a fraction of a second. Never put a finger between the jaws of
    a powered gripper. Keep hands away during calibration, which moves the jaws over the whole stroke without any
    command from you.

!!! warning "Start low"
    Test every new setup with a low current and speed: current 300 mA, speed 30. Raise them step by step once
    the application behaves; [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/) says what each value means.

!!! warning "Objects"
    A gripped object that slips, or that the jaws crush, can fly or fall. The grip force is a current limit, not a
    measurement: a hard object takes the full force, a soft one deforms until the force is reached.

!!! warning "Hair, clothing and jewellery"
    The jaws catch more than fingers: long hair, loose sleeves, gloves, lanyards, rings and bracelets. Tie back
    long hair and take off what can be caught before you work at a powered gripper, and keep it out of the jaws'
    reach while they move. Wear safety glasses where a part can slip out of the grip and fly.

## Electrical

!!! danger "The cable"
    The gripper's M8 connector carries 24 V next to the CAN bus. A cable with the wrong pinout destroys the driver:
    the cable of the other Source Robotics robot reverses the supply, and a self-made one with a wrong pin can
    put 24 V on a CAN pin. Use the cable
    made for your robot or check every pin of your own; see [The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/cable/).

!!! warning "Supply"
    24 V DC. The driver inside tolerates 12 to 29 V, but the gripper's force and speed figures assume 24 V.

!!! warning "Do not unplug a powered gripper"
    Connect and disconnect the cable with the supply off. Hot-plugging the connector can damage the driver.

!!! warning "Static"
    Static electricity damages the Spectral Micro driver inside the body. Unplug the supply and touch earthed metal
    before you open the body, set the termination switch or handle the driver, and hold the board by its edges.

## Temperature

The motor has a thermistor in its windings. At 75 °C the driver raises a temperature error and the gripper goes
idle; it clears when the motor has cooled and the error is cleared. A gripper holding an object at a high current
for long heats up: a hold at 300 mA ran for 24 hours at 62 °C, a hold at 1600 mA tripped the limit in four minutes
([Performance tests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/appendix/performance/)). For a long hold, use the lowest current that holds the object. A
self-built gripper without a thermistor in the windings has no protection and can burn out its motor; see
[Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/build/first-run/).

## Stopping the gripper

- The E-stop bit of the move command (`Send_gripper_data_pack`) stops the gripper and raises the gripper E-stop
  error. The error stays as long as the last command carries the bit: send a command with the bit at 0, then
  clear it ([Errors and recovery](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/errors/)).
- `Send_ESTOP` to the driver, or `#Idle` over UART, stops it as well.
- The CAN watchdog ([Send_Watchdog](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/reference/can/system/)) stops the gripper by itself when the host stops
  talking, which is the right protection for a program that may crash mid-grip.
- Cutting the supply releases the grip: a motor without current holds nothing beyond the mechanism's friction, so
  an object can drop.

None of these is a certified safety function. A machine that can hurt someone needs an emergency stop that cuts
the power, independent of the gripper and the robot software.

## Care

The gripper is not waterproof or dustproof: the rail and the racks are open to dust, chips and liquids. Keep it out
of wet or dusty places. What to check, and when to grease the mechanism, is in [Maintenance](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/07-maintenance/).

## Liability

The SSG-48 gripper is sold as a component for people who build their own machines, and its designs are published
for people who build the gripper itself. The hardware designs, the firmware and this documentation are under
development and may contain errors. Whoever builds or operates
a machine with the gripper is responsible for its safe design, assembly and operation. The
[full disclaimer](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/blob/main/SAFETY_WARNING_AND_DISCLAIMER.md)
is in the product repository.

# Specifications

## Electrical

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Supply voltage | 24 V DC; the driver tolerates 12 to 29 V, the force and speed figures assume 24 V |
| Idle power | 0.5 W |
| Motor current | set per move: up to 1500 mA for a grip, 300 mA for a long hold; see [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/) |
| Interface | CAN 2.0, 1 Mbit/s, 11-bit identifiers; node ID 0 as shipped |
| Connector | M8, 4 pins: 24 V, GND, CANH, CANL |
| CAN termination | 120 Ω, switchable; the switch is on the driver inside the body |
| Service port | the driver's UART, 3.3 V, 256000 baud, inside the body |
| Driver | Spectral Micro BLDC controller, field-oriented control, 14-bit encoder on the motor |
| Temperature protection | thermistor in the motor windings, 75 °C limit (changeable with `#Tlim`) |

## Mechanical

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Stroke | 48 mm |
| Grip force | ideal combined force up to about 80 N at 1500 mA; see the model assumptions in [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/) |
| Jaw speed | up to about 180 mm/s per jaw at speed 255; see [Force and speed](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/) |
| Position resolution | 1/255 of the stroke: 0.19 mm per step of the position byte |
| Mass | 440 g |
| Width | 104 mm over the jaw plates; 60.7 mm from the top of the jaw plates to the driver board, without a coupler connector |
| Drive | GBM5208-75 gimbal motor, pinion (6 mm pitch radius) on two racks, MGN7 linear rail |
| Grasps | external (closing on the object) and internal (opening inside a hollow object) |
| Mounting | coupler connectors for PAROL6 and PAR6, a UR5 adapter plate, a template for your own |
| Fingers | on the jaw plates' four-hole pattern; at most 80 mm tall and 60 mm wide |
| Body material | PETG, printed |

## Environmental

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Operating temperature | −5 to 65 °C |
| Protection | none: not waterproof or dustproof |

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/force-and-speed/ -->

# Force and speed

A move command carries a current limit in mA and a speed from 0 to 255. This page estimates the resulting
force and speed. Force and payload values are ideal model estimates, not measured ratings.

## Grip force

The driver limits the motor's current to the value you command, so the torque the motor produces is limited to
$T = K_t \, I_q$, with $K_t$ the motor's torque constant in Nm/A and $I_q$ the current limit in amperes (the
command is in mA).

The pinion shares that torque between two racks.
Here $F$ is the **combined normal force of both jaws**,
not the force at one jaw:

$$
F = \frac{K_t \, I_q}{r}, \qquad K_t = 0.325\ \text{Nm/A}, \quad r = 6\ \text{mm}
$$

$K_t$ = 0.325 Nm/A is the assumed torque constant used by this model and $r$ the pitch radius of the pinion.
They give an ideal combined force of about 54 N per ampere: about 8 N at 150 mA and 80 N at 1.5 A.

![The grip force against the current limit, from the formula above, up to the 1.5 A a grip uses](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/grip_force_light.webp){ width="820" }
![The grip force against the current limit, from the formula above, up to the 1.5 A a grip uses](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/grip_force_dark.webp){ width="820" }

The curve is computed from the assumed torque constant, rather than a measured force calibration. `#Kt`
over UART prints the driver's torque constant; that value must match its $q$-axis current convention.

A
datasheet current rating or supply current cannot be substituted directly. Measure your gripper with the
fingers and contact position you will use; below about 150 mA the motor does not move reliably.

The reported force-gauge result is about 48 N/A, but its per-jaw versus combined-force convention is not
specified. Keep it separate from the theoretical combined-force curve until the measurement setup is known.

The current limit caps motor torque; it does not guarantee that the commanded current or the estimated
contact force is reached. Mechanism friction, finger flex and the contact position affect the actual force.

!!! danger "Heat"
    The firmware clamps the gripper's current only at the driver's 2800 mA. A hold at 300 mA ran for 24 hours ([Performance tests](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/appendix/performance/));
    a hold at 1600 mA trips the 75 °C thermistor limit after four minutes. Use high currents for the grip and a
    low current for the hold.

For a symmetric grip, each jaw applies $F/2$. The torque balance is
$T = F_\mathrm{left} r + F_\mathrm{right} r = F r$; counting $F$ once for each jaw would count the motor's torque twice.
These are theoretical forces before losses in the mechanism.

A compression gauge between the jaws reads the
force at **one contact**; double that reading before comparing it with the combined force here. Record the
current, fingers and contact position when measuring; the same setup is needed for a useful comparison.

## Try it

<div class="gripper-calc" data-newtons-per-amp="54.2" data-radius-mm="6" data-ticks-min="40" data-ticks-max="80000" data-ticks-per-rev="16384" data-stroke-mm="48" markdown="0">
  <div class="gripper-calc__row">
    <label for="gc-current">Current limit of the move: <output data-out="current">300 mA</output></label>
    <input id="gc-current" type="range" name="current" min="100" max="1500" step="10" value="300">
  </div>
  <div class="gripper-calc__row gripper-calc__row--inline">
    <label for="gc-mu">Friction coefficient µ</label>
    <input id="gc-mu" type="number" name="mu" min="0.1" max="1.5" step="0.05" value="0.3">
    <label for="gc-safety">Safety factor</label>
    <input id="gc-safety" type="number" name="safety" min="1" max="5" step="0.5" value="2">
  </div>
  <p class="gripper-calc__result">Ideal combined grip force <strong data-out="force">16 N</strong> · estimated static payload <strong data-out="payload">0.25 kg</strong> with the chosen friction and safety factor</p>
  <div class="gripper-calc__row">
    <label for="gc-speed">Speed byte: <output data-out="speedbyte">30</output></label>
    <input id="gc-speed" type="range" name="speed" min="0" max="255" step="1" value="30">
  </div>
  <p class="gripper-calc__result">Each jaw <strong data-out="jaw">22 mm/s</strong> · the jaws close at <strong data-out="closing">43 mm/s</strong> · the full stroke takes <strong data-out="stroke">1.1 s</strong></p>
</div>

The formulas of this page, with your numbers: the force from the current, the weight held by friction with the
safety factor of the next section, and the speed from the speed byte.

## Payload

The grip force is not the weight the gripper can lift. An object held by friction between the two jaws is held
by $\mu(F_\mathrm{left} + F_\mathrm{right}) = \mu F$, with $\mu$ the friction coefficient between the fingers
and the object. Dividing the available friction force by a chosen safety factor $S$ gives the static estimate:

$$
W = \frac{\mu\,F}{S}, \qquad m = \frac{W}{g}
$$

Using an assumed $\mu$ = 0.3 and $S$ = 2, the model gives about 12 N of supported weight (1.2 kg) at 80 N
of combined grip force. This is a static estimate.

Upward acceleration of 1 g doubles the load; acceleration
and emergency-stop loads need a separate check. Friction can be lower than 0.3, so measure it with your
fingers on your object. A form-fit grip needs its own load assessment.

## Speed

The speed byte of a move is mapped by the firmware to the motor's speed in encoder ticks per second, linearly
from 40 at speed 0 to 80000 at speed 255:

$$
\text{ticks/s} = 40 + \frac{80000 - 40}{255}\, C
$$

The motor's encoder has 16384 ticks per revolution, so the angular speed is $\omega = \text{ticks/s} / 16384 \times 2\pi$
and each jaw moves at

$$
v = \omega \, r
$$

| Speed byte | Motor speed | Each jaw moves at | The jaws close at |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 40 ticks/s | 0.1 mm/s | 0.2 mm/s |
| 20 (the power-up default) | 6300 ticks/s, 0.4 rev/s | 15 mm/s | 29 mm/s |
| 30 | 9400 ticks/s, 0.6 rev/s | 22 mm/s | 43 mm/s |
| 128 | 40200 ticks/s, 2.5 rev/s | 92 mm/s | 185 mm/s |
| 255 | 80000 ticks/s, 4.9 rev/s | 184 mm/s | 370 mm/s |

Both jaws move, so the gap closes at twice the speed of one jaw. At full speed the 48 mm stroke takes well under a
quarter of a second. A move picks up speed over its first 0.1 s and slows down before the target, so a full open
or close at speed 255 takes about 0.3 s.

The gripper calibration runs at speed 40 and 500 mA, and reads each end under a light 100 mA push.

## Position

The position byte is linear over the stroke: 0 is the fully open end stop found by the gripper calibration, 255
the fully closed one.

Both lie a little inside their stop: 0 by 32 encoder ticks, 255 by 16, about 0.07 and 0.04 mm at each jaw. A
move to either end so arrives in free travel and does not press on the stop.

One step of the byte is 48 mm divided by 255, 0.19 mm. The driver considers the position reached within 5
encoder ticks, about 0.01 mm. It then holds without pushing while the jaws stay within a quarter of a step
(about 9 ticks).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/connector/ -->

# Connector and pinout

The gripper has one connector, an M8 4-pin male on the side of the body, and one cable: 24 V and the CAN bus.

![The M8 connector on the gripper body and its four signals: CANL, CANH, GND, 24V](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/GRPCON.webp){ width="700" }
![The M8 connector on the gripper body and its four signals: CANL, CANH, GND, 24V](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/GRPCON_dark.webp){ width="700" }

## Pin numbers

![M8 male on the gripper, as it sits in the gripper: the numbered signals](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/gripper-m8-face.svg){ width="650" }
![M8 male on the gripper, as it sits in the gripper: the numbered signals](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/gripper-m8-face_dark.svg){ width="650" }

The drawing shows the connector's staggered contact layout. Look **into the male connector on the gripper**, with
its pins visible: the mating face, where the cable plugs in. The female cable connector has the mirrored contact
view. Use the numbers moulded into the connector, rather than matching wire colours or the installed housing's
rotation.

| Gripper pin | Signal | Connection |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **CANL** | CAN low |
| **2** | **CANH** | CAN high, 1 Mbit/s with CANL |
| **3** | **+24 V** | positive motor supply |
| **4** | **GND** | power-supply return |

These are the numbers of the mating face, the side you connect to.

!!! note "Building the gripper: the solder side"
    Page 17 of the [assembly manual](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/blob/main/Assembly%20manual/Gripper_assembly_manual.pdf)
    numbers the other side of the same connector, where the wires are soldered when the gripper is built:
    1 24V, 2 CANL, 3 GND, 4 CANH. Use those numbers for soldering only, and the table above for connecting.

They describe the **gripper end**. PAROL6 and PAR6 use different connections at the robot end:
[The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/cable/) gives both diagrams. Check continuity with the supply disconnected.

!!! danger "The wrong cable destroys the driver"
    A reversed supply or 24 V on a CAN pin destroys the driver inside the gripper the moment it is powered; the
    other robot's cable reverses the supply. Use the cable
    made for your robot; check a self-made cable pin by pin against the pinout above and the wiring diagram before you
    plug it in.

## Inside the body

The Spectral Micro driver's own connectors are inside, reachable when the coupler connector is unscrewed: its
UART port (3.3 V, JST SH, 4 pins), used to configure a self-built gripper ([Over UART](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/uart/)),
and its CAN termination switch ([CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/can-termination/)). The driver's pinout
is in the [Spectral Micro documentation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/latest/03-technical-data/connectors/).

## CAD

The STEP files of every part are in the product repository, the reference for anything that has to fit:

- [STEP files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files): the body parts
  (`Body`), the whole gripper (`Whole gripper`), the jaw plate template, the fin-ray fingers and the pinch jaws
  (`Jaws`), the generic coupler connector template and the UR5 adapter plate (`Couplers`).
- [Print files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/tree/main/Print%20files):
  the printable parts (STL) of both hardware versions (`V2`, `V1`), the fin-ray fingers and their jaw plate
  (`Jaws`), and the coupler connectors for PAROL6 and PAR6 (`Couplers`).

<div class="grid" markdown>

![The robot model of the SSG-48 with the fin-ray fingers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/renders/ssg48_fin_ray.webp){ width="380" }
![The robot model of the SSG-48 with the fin-ray fingers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/renders/ssg48_fin_ray_dark.webp){ width="380" }

![The robot model of the SSG-48 with the solid fingers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/renders/ssg48_solid.webp){ width="380" }
![The robot model of the SSG-48 with the solid fingers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/renders/ssg48_solid_dark.webp){ width="380" }

</div>

## For simulation

The product repository's [ssg48_description](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/tree/main/ssg48_description)
guide links the gripper's models, which are kept in [robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions):
standalone URDF and MJCF (MuJoCo) packages of the gripper with solid or fin-ray jaws, with their meshes, collision
shapes and mass properties, and the PAROL6 and PAR6 models with the gripper mounted.

[CAD and downloads](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/cad-files/) lists everything that can be downloaded.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/integration-data/ -->

# Data for robot integration

What a robot's software needs to carry the gripper: the frame it is mounted by, the mass, the centre of mass, the
inertia and the tool centre point (TCP).

The numbers come from the gripper's URDF and MJCF (MuJoCo) models in
[robot_descriptions](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions/tree/v2.18.1), version 2.18.1,
moved into the frame below; the two files give the same values. Both models are on
[CAD and downloads](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/cad-files/).

## The frame

The origin is the centre of the mounting face, on the coupler side: the plane where the robot's flange meets the
gripper, and the `flange` frame of the URDF and MJCF models. On PAROL6 it is the flange face, 50.5 mm from the
joint 6 centre ([Dimensions and kinematics](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/latest/03-technical-data/kinematics/)).

- **Z** points out of the mounting face, through the body to the fingers: the approach direction. On the robot it
  is the flange's Z.
- **Y** is the jaw travel: the jaws move apart and together along Y, symmetrically about Z.
- **X** is square to both, across the 31.4 mm width of the jaw plates. The M8 connector on the body points along
  X.

## Mass and inertia

The centre of mass in mm, the inertia in kg·m² about the centre of mass, with axes parallel to the frame, for
fully open jaws.

| Fingers | Mass, measured | Mass in the model | Centre of mass x, y, z | Ixx, Iyy, Izz | Ixy, Ixz, Iyz |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pinch jaws (the model's Solid jaws, `ssg48_solid`) | 440 g | 440.0 g | 0.06, 0.14, 25.71 | 2.615e-4, 1.220e-4, 2.245e-4 | -6.14e-6, -2.69e-6, 0.86e-6 |
| Fin-ray fingers (`ssg48_fin_ray`) | 440 g | 440.0 g | 0.06, 0.14, 25.71 | 2.615e-4, 1.220e-4, 2.245e-4 | -6.14e-6, -2.69e-6, 0.86e-6 |

The jaws do not move the centre of mass: they travel symmetrically. Closing them brings each finger 23.5 mm
towards the Z axis, which lowers Ixx and Izz by about 0.65e-4 kg·m² at the closed end.

## Tool centre point

| Fingers | x, y, z | Orientation | Opening | The point |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pinch jaws | 0, 0, 91.4 mm | the frame's: roll, pitch and yaw 0 | any | the middle between the finger tips, where the tips meet when the jaws close |
| Fin-ray fingers | 0, 0, 114.8 mm | the frame's: roll, pitch and yaw 0 | any, with the fingers unloaded | the middle between the finger tips |

The point stays on the Z axis at every opening, because the jaws move symmetrically. The middle of the gripping
faces is lower: at z = 75.9 mm for the pinch jaws (faces from 60.4 to 91.4 mm) and 87.6 mm for the fin-ray
fingers (60.4 to 114.8 mm).

The models have one `tcp` frame for both finger types, at 0, 0, 83.8 mm with the frame's orientation; the PAROL6
and PAR6 robot models move it (on PAROL6, a6 = 134.3 mm = 50.5 + 83.8 mm).

robot_descriptions keeps it as a control frame, not a measured grasp centre: it is 7.6 mm short of the pinch tips
and 31.0 mm short of the fin-ray tips.

## How accurate the numbers are

The masses are measured: 440 g for the whole gripper, 39.3 g for each moving assembly (carriage, jaw and finger)
and 361.4 g for the rest.

The centre of mass and the inertia are not: robot_descriptions
(2.18.1, [MODEL_DETAILS.md](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/robot_descriptions/tree/v2.18.1/docs/maintenance/MODEL_DETAILS.md))
says that the gripper COM and central inertia remain unverified estimates. Both finger types share one set of mass
properties in the model, so the two rows are the same.

In both files each finger's centre of mass lies on the
other side of the Z axis from the finger, and 8 to 13 mm closer to the mounting face than the finger meshes'
centres: the open-jaw values above come out close, but the files' own inertia at other openings is not reliable.

The geometry, and with it the frame and the finger tips, is the CAD's.

## Where the numbers go

On PAROL6, `rbt.select_tool("SSG-48")` (with `variant_key="pinch"` for the pinch jaws) sets the Python API's own
TCP for the gripper, and `set_tcp_offset` or `set_tcp_transform` moves it
([Tools and the TCP](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/latest/programming/02-python-api/tools-and-tcp/));
in a URDF, the frame is a fixed joint from the robot's flange, the mass table an `<inertial>` and the TCP a
`tcp` link, as in the models' `ssg48_description` package.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/ -->

# Installation

Putting the gripper on a robot: the mounting, the cable that carries its power and its CAN bus, the jaws for
your objects, and the CAN termination.

When all of it is done, continue with [First setup](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/05-setup/).

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/mounting/ -->

# Mounting on a robot

The gripper mounts by its coupler connector, the round part on the back of the body. The repository has three,
for PAROL6, PAR6 and the UR5 flange, and a STEP template for your own.

| Robot | Part | Where |
|---|---|---|
| PAROL6 | `coupler_connector_PAROL6.STL` | [Print files/Couplers](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/tree/main/Print%20files/Couplers) |
| PAR6 | `coupler_connector_PAR6.STL` | the same folder |
| UR5 | `UR_coupler_gripper.STEP` | [STEP files/Couplers](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Couplers) |
| your own | `coupler_connector_generic_STEP.STEP`, the template | the same folder |

![The generic coupler connector template: the bolt circle of the gripper on the outside, your flange's pattern in the middle](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/Capture.webp){ width="520" }
![The generic coupler connector template: the bolt circle of the gripper on the outside, your flange's pattern in the middle](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/Capture_dark.webp){ width="520" }

## PAROL6

The PAROL6 coupler connector carries a shaft coupler with an 8 mm bore and two M4 clamp screws for the robot's
last joint, and the homing tab that joint 5 homes against.

1. Fit `coupler_connector_PAROL6` to the gripper, with the homing tab on the same side as the gripper's cable
   connector and an M3 × 12 screw in the marked hole, as the last pages of the
   [assembly manual](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/blob/main/Assembly%20manual/Gripper_assembly_manual.pdf)
   show.
2. Slide the gripper onto the J6 motor shaft.
3. Tighten the two screws of the shaft coupler, one on each side, with blue threadlocker.
4. Connect the [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) to the gripper and to
   the robot's gripper port ([The cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/cable/)).

<div class="grid" markdown>
![The gripper on the J6 shaft](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/gripper_parol1.webp){ width="400" }
![The coupler screws](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/gripper_parol4.webp){ width="400" }
</div>

The PAROL6 software needs to know the gripper is there, and the control board firmware needs the joint 5
homing offset for it: [On PAROL6 and PAR6](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/robots/).

## PAR6

`coupler_connector_PAR6` bolts to the PAR6 wrist; the PAR6 gripper cable, wired differently from the PAROL6 one,
goes to the robot's tool connector.

## Another robot

Adapt the template to your flange, or use the UR5 adapter plate as a starting point. Keep the gripper's connector
reachable, and route the cable so that it cannot be pulled by the robot's motion.

## On the bench

For testing, clamp the body, not the jaw plates or the rail, and leave the whole stroke free: calibration moves
the jaws from one end stop to the other without any command from you.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/cable/ -->

# The cable

![PAROL6 and PAR6 gripper cables are not interchangeable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/cable_warning.svg){ width="1000" }

One cable with an M8 4-pin connector powers the gripper and carries its CAN bus. The robot end differs from robot
to robot.

!!! danger "PAROL6 and PAR6 cables are different"
    The two robots put the four signals on different pins of their gripper port. The PAROL6 cable in a PAR6, or
    the other way round, reverses the gripper's supply, 24 V on its GND pin, and destroys its driver. Use the cable sold for your
    robot, and check a self-made cable pin by pin.

## The cables from the shop

| Robot | Cable |
|---|---|
| PAROL6 | [PAROL6 gripper cable](https://source-robotics.com/products/gripper-cable) |
| PAR6 | the PAR6 gripper cable, coming to the shop |

## Making your own

For a bench setup, another robot, or a replacement, the cable is four wires between an M8 4-pin female connector
at the gripper and whatever the other end needs:

| Part | Quantity | BOM |
|---|---|---|
| 26 AWG 4-wire twisted-pair cable, 0.15 mm², shielded | about 0.4 m | [cable](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_c4m3ggwn) |
| M8 4-pin female cable connector (the gripper has the male) | 1 | [connector](https://s.click.aliexpress.com/e/_c4OWHPKF) |
| M8 4-pin male cable connector, for a robot with an M8 port | 1 | the same listing |

<div class="grid" markdown>
![The M8 male connector](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/M8_male.webp){ width="260" }
![The M8 female connector](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/M8_female.webp){ width="260" }
![A finished cable](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/cable_assembly.webp){ width="340" }
</div>

Wire it as the diagram for your robot shows. Pin 1 to 4 are the numbers moulded into the M8 connectors; the
colours are those of the cable in the BOM.

=== "PAROL6"
    ![The PAROL6 cable: the pins are crossed between the two ends](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/PAROL6_cable.webp){ width="320" }

    Male end at the robot, female end at the gripper. The cable mirrors the CAN pair and the power pair between its
    ends, so each signal reaches the gripper's pin for the same signal: +24 V to +24 V, GND to GND, CANH to CANH,
    CANL to CANL. Wire a cable of your own by signal, and check each end against its own pin table: the PAROL6
    [gripper socket](https://docs.source-robotics.com/PAROL-docs/latest/end-effectors/flange/#the-gripper-socket)
    and the gripper's [pin numbers](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/connector/#pin-numbers).

=== "PAR6"
    ![The PAR6 cable: pin to pin](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/PAR6_cable.png){ width="200" }

=== "Bench or your own robot"
    Connect the gripper's 24V and GND to a 24 V supply and its CANH and CANL to your CAN interface; on a PC that
    is the CANvas adapter's CAN terminals. [Connector and pinout](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/03-technical-data/connector/) shows which
    pin of the gripper's connector is which signal. Twist the CAN pair, keep the cable short at 1 Mbit/s, and
    terminate the bus at both ends ([CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/can-termination/)).

Connect the shield at one end only. Check continuity and the absence of shorts between all four pins before the
first power-up.

## Handling

Plug and unplug with the supply off. Route the cable along the robot with enough slack for the wrist's full
motion, and keep it away from the jaws' travel.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/jaws/ -->

# Jaws

The gripper's two jaw plates carry a four-hole pattern for fingers. The product repository has fingers to print
and a template for your own.

![The jaw plate template, with the four mounting holes](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/jaw_plate.PNG){ width="520" }

| Fingers | Files | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Fin-ray fingers | `fin_ray_1`, `fin_ray_3`, `Finger_1` and `Jaw_plate_fin_ray` in the `Jaws` folders of [Print files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/tree/main/Print%20files/Jaws) and [STEP files](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Jaws) | fingers that wrap around round and irregular objects; printed in a flexible filament |
| Pinch jaws | `solid_jaws_pinch` and `solid_jaws_pinch_foam` in [STEP files/Jaws](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-48-adaptive-electric-gripper/tree/main/STEP%20files/Jaws) | solid jaws for small and flat objects, with or without a foam pad |
| Your own | `Jaw_plate.STEP`, the template | keep the hole pattern, shape the rest |

## Limits

- Fingers at most **80 mm** tall and **60 mm** wide: longer fingers multiply the lever arm on the jaw plates
  and the rail, and foul the body at full opening.
- The grip force is set at the finger faces. A finger that bends takes some of it.

!!! warning "Custom fingers on a PAR6"
    On a PAR6, custom fingers must keep the size of the original fingers: no longer, no wider and no thicker.
    The PAR6 software works with the gripper's original dimensions (its collision model of the tool and the
    tool centre point), so a larger finger reaches where the robot does not expect it.

## Calibrate after changing the fingers

The gripper calibration finds the end stops with the fingers fitted; fingers that meet earlier or later than the
old ones change where 255 is. Calibrate again after a change, which happens at the next power-up anyway.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/can-termination/ -->

# CAN termination

A CAN bus needs a 120 Ω resistor at each of its two ends. The gripper's driver has one, on a switch. The gripper
is normally the last node on a robot's bus, where the switch must be **ON**.

| The gripper is | Switch |
|---|---|
| the last node on a robot's bus, at the end of the arm | ON |
| alone on a bench bus with the CANvas adapter (which has its own termination) | ON |
| in the middle of a bus, with other nodes after it | off |

To change it:

1. Unplug the supply.
2. Touch earthed metal (static electricity damages the driver).
3. Unscrew the coupler connector: the switch is on the Spectral Micro driver inside the body, next to its CAN
   connectors.
4. Set the switch; **ON** connects the resistor.

The driver's [connector page](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/latest/03-technical-data/connectors/)
shows where it is on the board.

A bus with the right termination measures about 60 Ω between CANH and CANL with everything unpowered. A missing
or doubled termination shows up as lost frames and a gripper that answers only sometimes.

!!! success "Check"
    About 60 Ω between CANH and CANL, unpowered. About 120 Ω: one end is not terminated; about 40 Ω: three
    terminations are on.


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/05-setup/ -->

# First setup

For the complete bench procedure, use the [one-page quick start](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/quick-start/).

From a mounted and cabled gripper to one that opens and closes on command. Motor GUI in the browser is the usual
tool for it; every step also gives the Python call and the UART command.

1. [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/05-setup/motor-gui/): the browser, the CANvas adapter, connecting to the gripper, the gripper panel.
2. [Calibrate, activate, move](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/05-setup/first-moves/): the three things every session starts with, and the first grip.

A self-built gripper first needs its driver set up, which a bought one already has: [Driver setup and first run](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/build/first-run/)
in the build guide.

A gripper that has been through these pages is ready for [Operation](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/).


---

<!-- https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/05-setup/motor-gui/ -->

# Motor GUI

[Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/) is Source Robotics' tool for its drivers and for the grippers built on them: a
page in the browser that reaches the hardware through the browser's serial port access, so there is nothing to
install. With the CANvas adapter on the gripper's CAN bus it calibrates and activates the gripper, opens and closes
it, shows its state and plots its position and current. It is the recommended tool for the first setup and for
testing; everything it does is one CAN message, so what you learn here carries over to
[Python](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/06-operation/python/) and the other interfaces.

!!! note "The gripper GUI is legacy"
    The earlier [SSG-gripper-GUI](https://github.com/Source-Robotics/SSG-gripper-GUI), a Python program with a
    Windows build, still works with both grippers but is not developed further. Use Motor GUI.

## What you need

- A Chromium-based browser: Chrome, Edge, Brave or Opera. The serial port access Motor GUI relies on (Web Serial)
  is not in Firefox or Safari.
- The [CANvas adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/canvas-usb-to-can-adapter) in a USB port and on the
  gripper's CAN bus, with the bus terminated ([CAN termination](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/04-installation/can-termination/)), and the
  gripper powered.
- Nothing on the gripper itself: a bought gripper is ready. The browser's port access and the adapter's
  installation are described on the Spectral site, [Motor GUI](https://docs.source-robotics.com/Spectral-BLDC-docs/latest/05-setup/motor-gui/).

## Connecting

1. Open [motorgui.com](https://motorgui.com/). In the connection bar choose **CAN (slcan)** and the bitrate
   1 Mbit/s, then connect: the browser asks which serial port, pick the CANvas adapter.
2. Choose the gripper's node in the node picker: its CAN ID, 0 unless you changed it. Switch the bar from
   **Motor** to **Gripper**.
3. The gripper panel fills in as soon as the gripper's feedback arrives: calibrated or not, activated or not, the
   position, the current and the errors. While it says that it is waiting for feedback, check the node ID, the
   power and that the driver is in gripper mode.

!!! success "Check"
    The gripper panel shows the position and the current, and *Not calibrated* after a power-up. If it keeps
    waiting for feedback: [The gripper does not answer](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/09-troubleshooting/#the-gripper-does-not-answer).

The panel works with one gripper at a time; to work with another on the same bus, pick its node. The **Motor**
side of the switch shows the same driver as a motor, which the gripper does not need.

## Try it without a gripper

Open [Motor GUI](https://motorgui.com/), choose **Mock CAN (demo)** and **Connect**, then switch to **Gripper**.
The whole panel runs in the browser without an adapter or a gripper. The mock device identifies itself as
SSG-48; MSG uses the same controls.

## The gripper panel

<figure class="gui-shot" markdown="1">
<div class="gui-shot__image" markdown="1">

![Calibrated and activated gripper demo with command controls and plots](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/assets/motor-gui/gripper-ready-demo.jpg){ width="1000" }

<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:1%;top:17%" aria-hidden="true">1</span>
<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:1%;top:54%" aria-hidden="true">2</span>
<span class="gui-shot__mark" style="left:88%;top:17%" aria-hidden="true">3</span>

</div>
<figcaption markdown="1">**1. State:** calibrated, activated, and no errors. **2. Commands:** position, speed and current, each applied with its Set button. **3. Plots:** position and current feedback. Captured from the **SSG-48 mock demo**; MSG uses the same controls.</figcaption>
</figure>

| Control | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Calibrate** | runs the gripper calibration: the jaws travel the whole stroke to find the end stops. The panel asks you to confirm; clear any error, deactivate the gripper and take everything out of the jaws first. Press nothing else until the panel says *Calibrated*: a move or **Clear errors** during the calibration ends it |
| **Activate**, **Deactivate** | the activate bit: a calibrated gripper carries out moves only while it is activated |
| *Position*, *Speed*, *Current*, each with **Set** | the move: position 0 (open) to 255 (closed), speed 0 to 255, current limit 0 to 1500 mA, which is the force. Each **Set** sends its value together with the other two as last sent |
| **Open**, **Close** | a move to position 0 or 255 with the set speed and current |
| **Stop** | ends the move where the jaws are |
| **E-stop**, or ++esc++ | stops the gripper at once: the move command with the E-stop bit, after which the gripper reports the E-stop error until a command with the bit at 0 has been sent and the error cleared |
| **Clear errors** | clears the errors; an error whose cause remains comes straight back |
| Plots | position and current, live, with the requested position drawn in; the window and the scale are adjustable, and **Export CSV** saves a recorded run |
| Events | the feedback rate and the recent gripper events, with **Export events** for diagnostics |
| Cycle test | moves between two positions at a speed and a current, a number of times with a dwell: for endurance tests and demonstrations. Keep the tab visible while it runs |

## Presets for a self-built gripper

Connected over **UART** instead, through the [serial adapter](https://source-robotics.com/products/usb-to-serial-adapter)
on the driver's UART port, Motor GUI's setup page has tuned presets for the grippers: *SSG-48*, and the three *MSG*
steppers for the other gripper.

A preset writes the
motor's parameters, the loop gains, gripper mode, the thermistor and the CAN ID to the driver and saves them; its
CAN ID is 6, the PAR6 gripper's, so change it before applying for another robot.
[Driver configuration](https://docs.source-robotics.com/SSG48-gripper-docs/2/build/first-run/) says when to apply it, and lists the same settings as commands
for a terminal.

The *SSG-48* preset writes the same values on firmware 109 and 110.

Over CAN, Motor GUI 0.7.0 applies a preset whole on firmware 110: gripper mode, the thermistor and `#Rstint` go
out as parameters 92, 91 and 90. On 109 those three need UART.

## Calibration prompt

<figure class="gui-shot" markdown="1">
<div class="gui-shot__image" markdown="1">
